findings.title: High CPU on Dream Machine Pro (93%)
findings.summary: Dream Machine Pro is running at 93.4% CPU, which can cause latency and dropped features.
findings.recommendation: Identify heavy features (IDS/IPS, DPI, smart queues) and disable or right-size them; check for runaway processes after a firmware update, or upgrade the gateway if sustained at high WAN throughput.

findings.title: Garage AP is offline
findings.summary: Device Garage AP (UAP-AC-Lite) is not reachable by the controller.
findings.recommendation: Check power and PoE on the device's switch port, verify the uplink cable, and power-cycle the device. If it stays offline, factory-reset and re-adopt.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Living Room AP
findings.summary: Living Room AP is on 6.6.50 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Office Switch
findings.summary: Office Switch is on 6.6.10 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Access points run 2 different firmware versions
findings.summary: Roaming, band steering and fast-transition behaviour are negotiated between APs. When they run different firmware those features can behave inconsistently, producing dropouts that look like RF problems.
findings.recommendation: Bring every AP to the same version (currently 6.6.55) in one maintenance window rather than updating them piecemeal.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz on channel 3
findings.summary: Office AP uses 2.4 GHz channel 3; only channels 1, 6 and 11 are non-overlapping, so this channel interferes with two channel groups at once.
findings.recommendation: Set the 2.4 GHz radio to channel 1, 6 or 11 (pick the least used by neighbors).

findings.title: 2 APs share 2.4 GHz channel 6
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP all broadcast on 2.4 GHz channel 6; co-channel contention reduces airtime for every client.
findings.recommendation: Spread these APs across channels 1, 6 and 11.

findings.title: 2 APs share 5 GHz channel 149 at wide width
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP share 5 GHz channel 149 with 80 MHz+ width; wide overlapping channels amplify co-channel interference.
findings.recommendation: Assign distinct 5 GHz channels (e.g. 36/52/100/149) or reduce channel width to 40 MHz in dense deployments.

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100
findings.summary: Office AP broadcasts on channel 100, which requires radar detection. A radar event silences the radio for 30 minutes and every client on it is disconnected.
findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (22%)
findings.summary: 22.4% of transmissions on Office AP's 2.4 GHz radio are retries — a sign of interference, distant clients, or co-channel contention.
findings.recommendation: Fix the channel plan first (overlap/width findings), then check for non-WiFi interferers near this AP and consider raising minimum data rates.

findings.title: Patio AP is wirelessly meshed via Living Room AP
findings.summary: Patio AP uplinks through Living Room AP over the air. A meshed AP splits its radio time between serving clients and relaying, roughly halving throughput per hop.
findings.recommendation: Run Ethernet to this AP if at all possible. If it must stay meshed, keep it within one hop of a wired AP and make sure both radios see each other well above -65 dBm.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz width is 40 MHz
findings.summary: 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz consumes most of the band and almost always increases interference more than it adds throughput.
findings.recommendation: Set 2.4 GHz channel width to 20 MHz.

findings.recommendation: Move this network to WPA2/WPA3 transition mode. Watch for older IoT clients that cannot handle the management-frame protection WPA3 requires; if any break, keep them on a separate WPA2 network rather than reverting this one.

findings.recommendation: Move this network to WPA2/WPA3 transition mode. Watch for older IoT clients that cannot handle the management-frame protection WPA3 requires; if any break, keep them on a separate WPA2 network rather than reverting this one.

findings.title: PoE limited on Rack Switch port 5
findings.summary: Port 5 on Rack Switch is delivering limited PoE — the attached device may be underpowered, causing instability or reduced performance.
findings.recommendation: Check the switch's total PoE budget and the attached device's power class; move high-draw devices to a port/switch with headroom or use a PoE+ injector.

findings.title: Office AP port 1 linked at 100 Mbps (capable of 1000)
findings.summary: Port 1 on Office AP negotiated only 100 Mbps on a faster-capable link — the classic signature of a damaged cable or bad termination (a failed wire pair forces 100 Mbps).
findings.recommendation: Re-terminate or replace the cable on this port, then confirm it renegotiates at full speed. Also check for a forced-speed setting.

findings.title: 1 guest client(s) stuck unauthorized
findings.summary: Guest clients are connected but not authorized through the portal — they hold an association without network access.
findings.recommendation: Check the guest portal flow (captive portal reachability, voucher validity); authorize or disconnect these clients.

findings.title: High CPU on Dream Machine Pro (93%)
findings.summary: Dream Machine Pro is running at 93.4% CPU, which can cause latency and dropped features.
findings.recommendation: Identify heavy features (IDS/IPS, DPI, smart queues) and disable or right-size them; check for runaway processes after a firmware update, or upgrade the gateway if sustained at high WAN throughput.

findings.title: Garage AP is offline
findings.summary: Device Garage AP (UAP-AC-Lite) is not reachable by the controller.
findings.recommendation: Check power and PoE on the device's switch port, verify the uplink cable, and power-cycle the device. If it stays offline, factory-reset and re-adopt.

findings.title: Dream Machine Pro appears to be reboot-looping
findings.summary: Dream Machine Pro has shown under 24h uptime across 3 scans spanning more than a day — it is likely restarting repeatedly.
findings.recommendation: Check PoE budget on its switch port, inspect for overheating, and review firmware release notes; downgrade if a recent update introduced instability.

findings.title: Dream Machine Pro rebooted recently

findings.title: Firmware update available for Office Switch

findings.title: Access points run 2 different firmware versions

findings.title: 2 APs share 2.4 GHz channel 6

findings.title: 2 APs share 5 GHz channel 149 at wide width

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100

findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (22%)

findings.recommendation: Set 2.4 GHz channel width to 20 MHz.

findings.recommendation: Move the radio to 802.11n or later and disable legacy 802.11b data rates, unless a device on this network genuinely needs them.

findings.title: Patio AP is wirelessly meshed via Living Room AP
findings.summary: Patio AP uplinks through Living Room AP over the air. A meshed AP splits its radio time between serving clients and relaying, roughly halving throughput per hop.
findings.recommendation: Run Ethernet to this AP if at all possible. If it must stay meshed, keep it within one hop of a wired AP and make sure both radios see each other well above -65 dBm.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz width is 40 MHz
findings.summary: 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz consumes most of the band and almost always increases interference more than it adds throughput.
findings.recommendation: Set 2.4 GHz channel width to 20 MHz.

findings.title: Cameras is WPA2-only
findings.summary: Cameras accepts WPA2 alone. WPA3 closes the offline dictionary attack that WPA2's handshake allows, and the WPA2/WPA3 transition mode keeps older clients working while newer ones negotiate WPA3.
findings.recommendation: Move this network to WPA2/WPA3 transition mode. Watch for older IoT clients that cannot handle the management-frame protection WPA3 requires; if any break, keep them on a separate WPA2 network rather than reverting this one.

findings.title: Home-IoT is WPA2-only

findings.title: PoE limited on Rack Switch port 5
findings.summary: Port 5 on Rack Switch is delivering limited PoE — the attached device may be underpowered, causing instability or reduced performance.
findings.recommendation: Check the switch's total PoE budget and the attached device's power class; move high-draw devices to a port/switch with headroom or use a PoE+ injector.

findings.title: Office AP port 1 linked at 100 Mbps (capable of 1000)
findings.summary: Port 1 on Office AP negotiated only 100 Mbps on a faster-capable link — the classic signature of a damaged cable or bad termination (a failed wire pair forces 100 Mbps).
findings.recommendation: Re-terminate or replace the cable on this port, then confirm it renegotiates at full speed. Also check for a forced-speed setting.

findings.title: 1 guest client(s) stuck unauthorized
findings.summary: Guest clients are connected but not authorized through the portal — they hold an association without network access.
findings.recommendation: Check the guest portal flow (captive portal reachability, voucher validity); authorize or disconnect these clients.

findings.title: High CPU on Dream Machine Pro (93%)
findings.summary: Dream Machine Pro is running at 93.4% CPU, which can cause latency and dropped features.
findings.recommendation: Identify heavy features (IDS/IPS, DPI, smart queues) and disable or right-size them; check for runaway processes after a firmware update, or upgrade the gateway if sustained at high WAN throughput.

findings.title: Garage AP is offline
findings.summary: Device Garage AP (UAP-AC-Lite) is not reachable by the controller.
findings.recommendation: Check power and PoE on the device's switch port, verify the uplink cable, and power-cycle the device. If it stays offline, factory-reset and re-adopt.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Living Room AP
findings.summary: Living Room AP is on 6.6.50 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Office Switch
findings.summary: Office Switch is on 6.6.10 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Access points run 2 different firmware versions
findings.summary: Roaming, band steering and fast-transition behaviour are negotiated between APs. When they run different firmware those features can behave inconsistently, producing dropouts that look like RF problems.
findings.recommendation: Bring every AP to the same version (currently 6.6.55) in one maintenance window rather than updating them piecemeal.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz on channel 3
findings.summary: Office AP uses 2.4 GHz channel 3; only channels 1, 6 and 11 are non-overlapping, so this channel interferes with two channel groups at once.
findings.recommendation: Set the 2.4 GHz radio to channel 1, 6 or 11 (pick the least used by neighbors).

findings.title: 2 APs share 2.4 GHz channel 6
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP all broadcast on 2.4 GHz channel 6; co-channel contention reduces airtime for every client.
findings.recommendation: Spread these APs across channels 1, 6 and 11.

findings.title: 2 APs share 5 GHz channel 149 at wide width
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP share 5 GHz channel 149 with 80 MHz+ width; wide overlapping channels amplify co-channel interference.
findings.recommendation: Assign distinct 5 GHz channels (e.g. 36/52/100/149) or reduce channel width to 40 MHz in dense deployments.

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100
findings.summary: Office AP broadcasts on channel 100, which requires radar detection. A radar event silences the radio for 30 minutes and every client on it is disconnected.
findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (22%)

findings.recommendation: Assign distinct 5 GHz channels (e.g. 36/52/100/149) or reduce channel width to 40 MHz in dense deployments.

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100
findings.summary: Office AP broadcasts on channel 100, which requires radar detection. A radar event silences the radio for 30 minutes and every client on it is disconnected.
findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (22%)
findings.summary: 22.4% of transmissions on Office AP's 2.4 GHz radio are retries — a sign of interference, distant clients, or co-channel contention.
findings.recommendation: Fix the channel plan first (overlap/width findings), then check for non-WiFi interferers near this AP and consider raising minimum data rates.

findings.title: Patio AP is wirelessly meshed via Living Room AP
findings.summary: Patio AP uplinks through Living Room AP over the air. A meshed AP splits its radio time between serving clients and relaying, roughly halving throughput per hop.
findings.recommendation: Run Ethernet to this AP if at all possible. If it must stay meshed, keep it within one hop of a wired AP and make sure both radios see each other well above -65 dBm.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz width is 40 MHz
findings.summary: 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz consumes most of the band and almost always increases interference more than it adds throughput.
findings.recommendation: Set 2.4 GHz channel width to 20 MHz.

findings.title: High WAN latency (200 ms)

findings.title: WAN probe failures: 15% of connections

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz on channel 3

findings.title: 2 APs share 2.4 GHz channel 6

findings.title: 2 APs share 5 GHz channel 149 at wide width

findings.recommendation: Assign distinct 5 GHz channels (e.g. 36/52/100/149) or reduce channel width to 40 MHz in dense deployments.

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100
findings.summary: Office AP broadcasts on channel 100, which requires radar detection. A radar event silences the radio for 30 minutes and every client on it is disconnected.
findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (35%)

findings.recommendation: Fix the channel plan first (overlap/width findings), then check for non-WiFi interferers near this AP and consider raising minimum data rates.

findings.summary: 192.168.1.104/29 is a /29, which leaves 6 assignable addresses on a network that hands out DHCP leases.
findings.recommendation: Confirm this ceiling is intentional. If the network is meant to grow, widen the prefix now — renumbering later means re-addressing every static client.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz on channel 3
findings.summary: Office AP uses 2.4 GHz channel 3; only channels 1, 6 and 11 are non-overlapping, so this channel interferes with two channel groups at once.
findings.recommendation: Set the 2.4 GHz radio to channel 1, 6 or 11 (pick the least used by neighbors).

findings.title: 2 APs share 2.4 GHz channel 6
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP all broadcast on 2.4 GHz channel 6; co-channel contention reduces airtime for every client.
findings.recommendation: Spread these APs across channels 1, 6 and 11.

findings.title: 2 APs share 5 GHz channel 149 at wide width
findings.summary: APs Living Room AP, Patio AP share 5 GHz channel 149 with 80 MHz+ width; wide overlapping channels amplify co-channel interference.
findings.recommendation: Assign distinct 5 GHz channels (e.g. 36/52/100/149) or reduce channel width to 40 MHz in dense deployments.

findings.title: Office AP 5 GHz on DFS channel 100
findings.summary: Office AP broadcasts on channel 100, which requires radar detection. A radar event silences the radio for 30 minutes and every client on it is disconnected.
findings.recommendation: Move to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-165) unless the band is too congested to avoid DFS. If channels are auto-assigned, pin this radio manually — automatic selection keeps returning to DFS.

findings.title: High TX retries on Office AP 2.4 GHz (22%)
findings.summary: 22.4% of transmissions on Office AP's 2.4 GHz radio are retries — a sign of interference, distant clients, or co-channel contention.
findings.recommendation: Fix the channel plan first (overlap/width findings), then check for non-WiFi interferers near this AP and consider raising minimum data rates.

findings.title: Patio AP is wirelessly meshed via Living Room AP
findings.summary: Patio AP uplinks through Living Room AP over the air. A meshed AP splits its radio time between serving clients and relaying, roughly halving throughput per hop.
findings.recommendation: Run Ethernet to this AP if at all possible. If it must stay meshed, keep it within one hop of a wired AP and make sure both radios see each other well above -65 dBm.

findings.title: Office AP 2.4 GHz width is 40 MHz
findings.summary: 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz consumes most of the band and almost always increases interference more than it adds throughput.
findings.recommendation: Set 2.4 GHz channel width to 20 MHz.

findings.title: Cameras is WPA2-only
findings.summary: Cameras accepts WPA2 alone. WPA3 closes the offline dictionary attack that WPA2's handshake allows, and the WPA2/WPA3 transition mode keeps older clients working while newer ones negotiate WPA3.
findings.recommendation: Move this network to WPA2/WPA3 transition mode. Watch for older IoT clients that cannot handle the management-frame protection WPA3 requires; if any break, keep them on a separate WPA2 network rather than reverting this one.

findings.title: Home-IoT is WPA2-only

findings.title: PoE limited on Rack Switch port 5
findings.summary: Port 5 on Rack Switch is delivering limited PoE — the attached device may be underpowered, causing instability or reduced performance.
findings.recommendation: Check the switch's total PoE budget and the attached device's power class; move high-draw devices to a port/switch with headroom or use a PoE+ injector.

findings.title: Office AP port 1 linked at 100 Mbps (capable of 1000)
findings.summary: Port 1 on Office AP negotiated only 100 Mbps on a faster-capable link — the classic signature of a damaged cable or bad termination (a failed wire pair forces 100 Mbps).
findings.recommendation: Re-terminate or replace the cable on this port, then confirm it renegotiates at full speed. Also check for a forced-speed setting.

findings.title: 1 guest client(s) stuck unauthorized
findings.summary: Guest clients are connected but not authorized through the portal — they hold an association without network access.
findings.recommendation: Check the guest portal flow (captive portal reachability, voucher validity); authorize or disconnect these clients.

findings.title: High CPU on Dream Machine Pro (93%)
findings.summary: Dream Machine Pro is running at 93.4% CPU, which can cause latency and dropped features.
findings.recommendation: Identify heavy features (IDS/IPS, DPI, smart queues) and disable or right-size them; check for runaway processes after a firmware update, or upgrade the gateway if sustained at high WAN throughput.

findings.title: Garage AP is offline
findings.summary: Device Garage AP (UAP-AC-Lite) is not reachable by the controller.
findings.recommendation: Check power and PoE on the device's switch port, verify the uplink cable, and power-cycle the device. If it stays offline, factory-reset and re-adopt.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Living Room AP
findings.summary: Living Room AP is on 6.6.50 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Firmware update available for Office Switch
findings.summary: Office Switch is on 6.6.10 with an update available.
findings.recommendation: Review the release notes and update during a maintenance window. Keep all APs on the same firmware to avoid roaming quirks.

findings.title: Access points run 2 different firmware versions
findings.summary: Roaming, band steering and fast-transition behaviour are negotiated between APs. When they run different firmware those features can behave inconsistently, producing dropouts that look like RF problems.
findings.recommendation: Bring every AP to the same version (currently 6.6.55) in one maintenance window rather than updating them piecemeal.
